extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and patent counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria for when a court may judicially correct errors (typographical/clerical) in patent claim language as part of claim construction, including limits on evidence and examples of acceptable corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very demanding standard for judicial correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial correction of erroneous wording of a claim is proper only in narrow, demanding circumstances — e.g., when the intrinsic evidence clearly establishes that the error could only be reasonably understood in one way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court quotes precedent (Essex, Ultimax, CBT Flint, Novo, Group One, Pavo) and explains that correction is appropriate only when the construction is not subject to reasonable debate; the standard takes account of the public-notice function of patents and is applied de novo based entirely on intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error must be evident from the face of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: "The error must be 'evident from the face of the patent'" — i.e., obvious as determined 'from the point of view of one skilled in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence for obviousness comes from claim language, specification, and figures; if the claim grammar/logic plainly lacks antecedent or makes no sense, that supports evident error (example: backward reference to 'the connection profile of the second part' when no such antecedent exists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction must not be subject to reasonable debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction is appropriate only if 'the correction is not subject to reasonable debate based on consideration of the claim language and the specification and the prosecution history does not suggest a different interpretation of the claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court applies Novo/CBT Flint language: consider claim language and specification to determine whether only one reasonable correction exists; if reasonable parties could debate alternative constructions, judicial correction is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history must not suggest a different interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history must not indicate an interpretation inconsistent with the proposed judicial correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prosecution history suggests a different meaning, correction is inappropriate (contrast with Chef America where prosecution history weighed heavily). Here, lack of prosecution-history indication supports correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction limited to minor typographical/clerical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may correct 'obvious minor typographical and clerical errors in patents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correction should be textually simple and minor (e.g., restoring an omitted word) and must not amount to remaking the claim or changing substantive claim scope; Essex example: adding omitted word 'rear.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction must be textually simple and not change claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The correction should be 'textually simple' and should not alter the scope or meaning of the claims in a substantive way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections that significantly change claim context or scope are disallowed; however, if multiple reasonable alternatives have the same scope and meaning, a court may correct to the version that captures the intended scope (CBT Flint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of the reasonable correction (only one reasonable correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed correction must be the only reasonable correction a person skilled in the art would adopt from the intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must show the correction (e.g., changing 'second' to 'first') is the unique reading that the claim language and specification compel; alternative corrections that would alter meaning are not acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis requirement as a trigger for indefiniteness/correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims require proper antecedent basis; a missing antecedent (e.g., introducing 'the connection profile of the second part' without prior mention) can render a phrase indefinite or demonstrate an evident clerical error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a backward-referring 'the' lacks an antecedent in the claim, a skilled reader will note the anomaly; courts assess whether that anomaly evidences an obvious error correctable by construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence; limited role for extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim interpretation and judicial correction depend on intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); extrinsic evidence (experts) plays a limited role and cannot override clear intrinsic conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should not rely on extrinsic evidence to alter intrinsic conclusions; expert testimony that merely repeats intrinsic points adds nothing. Teva/Phillips limits on expert evidence are invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of figures and specification to identify evident errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures and their descriptions are part of the intrinsic record and may make an error evident (e.g., figures labeling 'connection profile 16' as part of the first part while text attributes it to the second part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specification text contradicts figures or other specification passages, a skilled reader can treat the contradictory wording as an evident error and correct accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with PTO correction under 35 U.S.C. § 255
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability of PTO correction under 35 U.S.C. § 255 is relevant background: PTO corrections are prospective and can reach a broader class of errors, but a party's failure to seek PTO correction does not automatically preclude judicial correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts respect that PTO correction is prospective and covers errors not limited to obvious ones; however, a party's delay or PTO denial does not by itself show the error was not evident or that judicial correction is impermissible (PTO denial may be because requested change would alter scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using correction to 're-make' the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction cannot be 'in any real sense ... a re-making of the claim'—it must give the claim the meaning intended by the applicant and understood by the examiner, not craft a new claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essex principle: the correction must reflect what was intended and understood; courts must resist correcting into language that would supply substantive additions or omitted limitations beyond a simple textual fix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate rule for judicial correction
rubrics_metrics.description: If (1) the error is evident on the face of the patent, (2) the proposed correction is the only reasonable interpretation from intrinsic evidence, and (3) the change is minor/clerical/textually simple and the prosecution history does not compel a different meaning, then judicial correction is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aggregates the elements discussed by the court; the analysis is fact-specific and must be applied de novo using claim language, specification, figures, and prosecution history; court cited Scalia & Garner: correct when failing to do so would yield a disposition no reasonable person could approve.
